claim: Of the 103 passages in the pur- corpus at the stanza unit, 21 state a count of the fort word and 82 state none.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, 49 numeral rows over 30 passages, 29 adjudicated COUNTS-PUR over 21 distinct stanzas; built by 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-counts.py and rv-pur-counts-adjudicate.py
notes: Denominator 103 = the etymological pur- family at the stanza unit (106 tokens, 104 padas, 103 stanzas, 86 hymns). 82 of 103 is 79.6 percent of the corpus carrying NO count. Any statement of the form 'the Rigveda says there were N forts' is drawn from a fifth of the passages that mention forts at all.

claim: Among the 21 passages stating a count of forts, 100 is stated in 8, ninety-nine in 6, seven in 4, ninety in 2, and 'hundreds' (satani, plural) in 1; two of the ninety-nine passages add an ordinal 'the hundredth'.
notes: Counts sum to 21 distinct passages; the two 'hundredth' passages are inside the 99 set and are not counted twice. The constitution's four enumerated headings (90, 99, 100, other counts) are all attested, and 'other counts' resolves to seven and to the unbounded plural 'hundreds'.

claim: Ninety-nine is NOT the modal count of forts in the Rigveda. One hundred is, by 8 passages to 6.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv as PUR4J-002. 8 passages state 100 and 6 state 99; counting the plural 'hundreds' of RV 6.31.4 with the hundreds makes it 9 to 6.
notes: This answers directly the question the reconciliation brief left open at section 2.6 item 2 ('whether 99 is the modal count, the maximal count, or merely the most quotable'). It is neither modal nor maximal: 100, 'hundreds' and 1000 are all larger, and 100 is more frequent. It is the most quotable. The figure that titles the inherited RV-01 specification and the the-forts page headline is the second most common count in the corpus.

claim: Ninety-nine is never expressed by a single numeral. In all six passages it is two words, nava 'nine' and navati- 'ninety', joined by ca in three of them and separated by other words in four.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, expression column. RV 1.54.6d puro navatim dambhayo nava; 2.19.6c navatim ca nava; 4.26.3b nava sakam navatih; 7.19.5b nava yat puro navatim ca; 7.99.5b nava puro navatim ca; 8.93.2a nava yo navatim puro
notes: The reconciliation brief section 2.6 item 1 flagged that 'even 99 is attested is a claim about a reading'. Tested here and upheld: the reading is secure, because all three full-coverage translators independent of one another on this point (Griffith, Geldner, Grassmann) render 99 at all six, and the padapatha analyses the words separately. But the object is a two-word expression, not a numeral.

claim: navati- 'ninety' is a feminine SINGULAR collective governing a plural puras in five of the six ninety-nine passages; only at RV 4.26.3 does it appear as an agreeing plural navatih.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, numeral_morph column: case=ACC|gender=F|number=SG at RV 1.54.6, 2.19.6, 7.19.5, 7.99.5, 8.93.2 and at the two ninety passages 1.130.7 and 3.12.6; case=ACC|gender=F|number=PL at RV 4.26.3
notes: Consequence for method, not only for grammar: a numeral-noun AGREEMENT test scored on case, gender and number under-reports navati- by construction, returning PARTIAL for a numeral that governs its noun perfectly well. Six rows of the counts register record this override explicitly. A mechanical agreement test run without this correction would drop five of the six ninety-nine passages.

claim: The identical nava-plus-navati- expression counts RIVERS, not forts, at RV 10.104.8, in a stanza that also carries the fort-word epithet purbhid.
locator: RV 10.104.8c navatim srotya nava ca sravantir; padapatha navatim | srotyah | nava | ca | sravantih. Griffith 'nine-and-ninety flowing streams'; Geldner 'die neunundneunzig fliessenden Stroeme'; Grassmann 'Die neunundneunzig Fluesse'. purbhit in pada b is NOM.SG.M, an epithet of Indra, and takes no numeral.
notes: The control case for the whole counts unit. It is also the case that defeats a stanza-level co-occurrence measure: navati- and a pur- family lemma share this stanza, and the ninety-nine here has nothing to do with forts. 04-AUDITS/rigveda-pur-family-method.md section 7 measured navati- at 33.5x its corpus rate inside family stanzas and declined to read it; this row is why that restraint was correct.

claim: Sambara's forts are counted at ninety, ninety-nine, one hundred, 'the hundredth' and 'hundreds' across six passages. Every count value the constitution section 4J enumerates attaches to this one opponent.
locator: RV 1.130.7 ninety (sambaram in pada d); 2.14.6 one hundred (satam sambarasya puro); 2.19.6 ninety-nine (sambarasya); 4.26.3 ninety-nine plus the hundredth (sambarasya); 6.31.4 'hundreds' (satani sambarasya puro); 7.99.5 ninety-nine (sambarasya)
notes: A measurement, and the sharpest single piece of evidence in this unit. The count is not a stable property of the opponent it is most often attached to. Recorded as a count of passages, not as an interpretation of why they differ; what it implies is PUR4J-012.

claim: In two of the six ninety-nine passages the ninety-nine is immediately followed by an ordinal 'the hundredth', applied to a dwelling word rather than to the fort word.
locator: RV 4.26.3: pada a-b nava sakam navatih ... purah, pada c satatamam vesyam 'the hundredth dwelling/inhabitant'. RV 7.19.5: pada b nava yat puro navatim ca, pada c nivesane satatama 'the hundredth in the settlement'.
notes: The ninety-nine and the hundredth are one schema: ninety-nine plus one completes a hundred. Note that satatama- does not modify pur- in either passage, so a search for numerals attached to the fort word alone would miss the completion that gives the ninety-nine its shape.

claim: Every count of forts in the corpus is one of seven, ninety, ninety-nine, one hundred or 'hundreds'. No passage states an irregular figure.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-counts.csv, count_of_forts over all 29 COUNTS-PUR rows. The numeral inventory of the 103 passages was fixed independently by scanning the Grassmann gloss of all 721 distinct lemmas occurring in them for a German number word, returning 12 candidates, all adjudicated.
notes: Stated with its denominator: this is a property of the 21 counting passages, and the numeral inventory it is drawn from was built by an exhaustive scan of the corpus's own lexicon, not by looking for the numbers already expected. Two gloss-scan candidates were excluded with reasons recorded in 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-counts.py: satakratu- (an Indra epithet) and arya- (a false positive matching 'drei' inside Grassmann's gloss 'Angehoeriger der drei oberen Grosskasten').

claim: The 'seven forts' passages cluster with Purukutsa and the Puru, and the ninety-nine and one hundred passages with Divodasa, Atithigva and Sambara. The count co-varies with the narrative cycle, not with the opponent alone.
locator: Seven: RV 1.63.7 (purukutsa-, puru-, sudas-), 1.174.2 (purukutsa-), 6.20.10 (purukutsa-, puru-), 7.18.13 (puru-) — Purukutsa or Puru in all four. Ninety-nine and one hundred: divodasa- at RV 1.53.8, 1.130.7, 2.19.6, 4.26.3, 4.30.20, 6.31.4; sambara- at RV 1.130.7, 2.14.6, 2.19.6, 4.26.3, 6.31.4, 7.99.5.
notes: Cuts against a reading in which the numbers are freely interchangeable ornament: they are distributed by story, and 'seven autumnal forts' is close to verbatim at RV 1.174.2b and 6.20.10c. Lemma co-presence in a stanza, not a claim that any named figure is patron or opponent of that passage; the roles are established per passage in the fields register, not here.

claim: Among the counting passages, the seven-fort set is the most Archaic on Arnold's periodisation (3 of 4 Archaic) and the ninety-nine set is predominantly Strophic (4 of 6).
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-passages.csv joined to rigveda-pur-counts.csv. Seven: RV 1.63.7 A, 1.174.2 A, 6.20.10 A, 7.18.13 C. Ninety-nine: RV 1.54.6 C, 2.19.6 A, 4.26.3 S, 7.19.5 S, 7.99.5 S, 8.93.2 S.
notes: Small n, and carrying every caveat that already caps the stratum column: it rests on Arnold 1905 alone (DEP-001), the by-book second instrument returns a null (DEP-004), and PUR-028 holds at HYPOTHESIS that Arnold's periods are chronological stages at all. With n=4 and n=6 this is a description of ten passages and NOT a chronology of the fort count. It is recorded so that a later unit cannot present it as new.

claim: Exactly three lemmas describe the material of a pur- in the Rigveda: ayasa- 'of metal' in 8 passages, asmanmaya- 'of stone' in 1, and ama- 'raw, unbaked' in 1. Ten of 103 passages state a material at all.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-fields.csv, material column. ayasa-: RV 1.58.8, 2.20.8, 4.27.1, 7.3.7, 7.15.14, 7.95.1, 8.100.8, 10.101.8. asmanmaya-: RV 4.30.20. ama-: RV 2.35.6. Descriptors identified by full case-gender-number agreement with a pur- family token; 04-AUDITS/rv-pur-fields.py
notes: 93 of 103 passages state no material. Typed NOT PRODUCED: a hymn praising the breaking of a fort had no occasion to say what it was built of, and the silence is not evidence that the poets did not know or that the forts were insubstantial.

claim: Seven of the eight metal forts are protective, mythic or metaphorical. Only RV 2.20.8 is an enemy's. Two passages identify a deity or a river AS the fort.
locator: RV 1.58.8 Agni asked to protect the singer WITH iron forts; 2.20.8 Indra casts down the Dasyus' iron forts (the only enemy fort); 4.27.1 a hundred iron forts CONFINE the speaking eagle; 7.3.7 Agni asked to protect us with a hundred iron forts; 7.15.14 'pur bhava satabhujih' — Agni asked to BE an iron pur; 7.95.1 'sarasvati dharunam ayasi puh' — the river Sarasvati IS an iron pur; 8.100.8 the falcon escapes the iron fort; 10.101.8 'purah krnudhvam ayasir adhrsta' — priests told to MAKE iron forts.
notes: The measurement that bears hardest on constitution section 4J's instruction not to translate pur automatically into a Mature Harappan city. The metal forts are overwhelmingly not enemy settlements, and in two passages the fort is a god or a river. A reading that takes ayasa- pur- as evidence of metal-using fortified settlements has to account for the seven, not only the one.

claim: The single stone fort and the single unbaked fort point opposite ways: asmanmaya- at RV 4.30.20 is an enemy's, ama- at RV 2.35.6 is a refuge.
locator: RV 4.30.20 'satam asmanmayinam puram indro vy asyat / divodasaya dasuse' — Indra overthrew a hundred stone forts for Divodasa. RV 2.35.6 'amasu pursu paro apramrsyam na aratayo vi nasan' — in the raw/unbaked forts neither malice nor deceptions reach him.
notes: Two passages, one lemma each. Recorded as two data points and not as a pattern: with n=1 on each side no distribution follows. ama- 'raw, ungekocht' is the one lemma in the corpus that could bear on building technique (unbaked earth), and it occurs once, in a passage about being unreachable rather than about construction.

claim: The corpus names exactly one fort. RV 1.149.3 has puram narminim, and Grassmann glosses narmin- as 'Name (oder Beiwort) einer pur-' — name or epithet of a pur.
locator: RV 1.149.3a 'a yah puram narminim adided'. Geldner: 'Der die Burg Narmini beschien'. Griffith: 'He who hath lighted up the joyous castle'.
notes: Griffith reads narmini- as an adjective ('joyous') and Geldner as a proper name ('the fort Narmini'). Grassmann's own gloss declines to choose. So the claim that the Rigveda names a fort rests on one word whose word-class is disputed by the two translators, and the register records the dispute rather than resolving it. If Geldner is right this is the only named fort in 103 passages; if Griffith is right there are none.

claim: Geldner's per-hymn group heading names a poet for 55 of the 103 passages and a deity or a metre for the other 48.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-fields.csv, poet_lineage and poet_lineage_basis. 33 distinct headings; the largest are '2. group: hymns to Indra' (26 passages) and '1. group: hymns to Agni' (11), both of which name a deity.
notes: The 48 are typed NOT PRODUCED, not anonymous: Geldner's headings are an arrangement, and where he arranged by deity he recorded no poet. The 55 that do carry a name carry it at three removes from composition — Geldner 1951 follows the Anukramani tradition, which post-dates the text. HOLD-006 records that no source independent of Geldner was reachable: GRETIL, archive.org and TITUS all returned 403 at the proxy (SRC-080 to SRC-083), having each returned 200 earlier the same day.

claim: Of the 103 passages: 17 carry a water lemma, 13 a cattle lemma, 12 a treasure lemma, 7 a mountain lemma, and 6 a named river, which is the Sindhu in all six.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-fields.csv. Water led by ap- (8) and sindhu- (6); cattle by gav- ~ go- (5) and vraja- (3); treasure by dhana- (2) and rayi- ~ ray- (2); mountain by adri- (3) and giri- (2). Named rivers: sindhu- in 6 passages, sarasvant- in 1.
notes: Presence of a lemma in a passage, not a claim that the fort had water, cattle or treasure in it. Each field was DEFINED before it was filled, by a rule over Grassmann's glosses for all 721 lemmas occurring in the passages. Two exclusions were needed and both changed the result: bahuvrihi 'having X' epithets (without which treasure returns 56 lemmas, mostly epithets of Indra) and owner words (without which pati- 'Herr, Gebieter, Besitzer' enters treasure in 5 passages on the string Besitz).

claim: Constitution section 4J's proposed geography field cannot be filled from the pinned corpus, which contains no geographic content of any kind.
locator: info/rv_locations.tsv and rv_locations.json, the files flagged in 06-BRIEFS/rv01-reconciliation.md section 4 as possibly bearing on this field. Columns: DOTS_AND_ZEROS, COMMAS_AND_ZEROS, DOTS, COMMAS, GRASSMANN, BOOK_INDEX, HYMN_INDEX, STANZA_INDEX. 10552 rows, one per stanza.
notes: A citation-format conversion table: 'location' means location in the text. Typed NOT PRODUCED - VedaWeb is a text edition and had no reason to carry geography. What the corpus CAN support is which hydronym lemmas occur in a passage (PUR4J-017), which is a textual fact; the step from a hydronym to a place on a map is a separate claim needing separate evidence, and is bounded by the research hold at Version 12 line 1175 against identifying the forts with one archaeological culture.

claim: Full morphological agreement identifies descriptors of the fort word in 43 passages within the same pada, 22 more within the same hemistich, and 23 more elsewhere in the stanza; two agreeing tokens are demonstrably not descriptors.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-fields.csv, three description columns plus agreeing_but_excluded. Excluded: RV 5.41.12 sruc- 'wooden sacrificial ladle', NOM.PL.F agreeing with purah but in a different clause; RV 7.6.2 adri- 'rock', GEN.SG.M agreeing with puramdarasya but belonging to 'they bring him from the mountain' two padas away.
notes: All three scopes are reported because each has a demonstrated failure and they fail in opposite directions. The pada scope MISSES ayasa- at RV 7.15.14, a predicate nominative two padas from its subject puh, which is the passage where the metal-fort image is clearest; it also misses asmanmaya- at RV 4.30.20 across a pada break. The stanza scope ADMITS the two false positives above. A single scope would have to choose which error to make.

claim: pur- is a feminine root noun. 67.5 percent of its 83 simplex tokens are accusative and 3.6 percent are locative: three tokens of 83.
locator: 03-REGISTERS/rigveda-pur-family-occurrences.csv, morphology column. ACC.PL puraḥ 45, ACC.SG puram 11 (56 of 83); LOC.SG puri 2, LOC.PL pursu 1 (RV 2.35.6c amasu pursu). Also GEN.PL puram 10, INS.PL purbhiḥ 6, NOM.SG puḥ 5, NOM.PL puraḥ 2, INS.SG pura 1.
notes: A measurement of case distribution, not an interpretation of it. Recorded because it is the single most awkward figure for any reading that makes pur- a settlement: the commonest thing a pur does in the Rigveda is be the direct object of a verb, and it is almost never a place anyone is said to be in.

claim: Grassmann's dictionary defines pur- as 'Wall aus Steinen und Lehm, Verschanzung, Palisade' — wall of stones and clay, entrenchment, palisade. Not a city, town or fortress.
locator: info/matched_lemmata.json in the SRC-069 clone, gloss for lemma pur-. Cognate glosses in the same source: puramdara- 'Zerstoerer der Waelle', purbhid- 'die Waelle aufbrechend', purohan- 'die Waelle zerschlagend', purpati- 'Herr der Burg', purya- 'in einem festen Platz befindlich'.
notes: This is the gloss that fixed the register's family boundary at PUR-006, so it is already load-bearing for the corpus's membership. Recorded as a claim in its own right because the standard nineteenth-century Rigveda lexicon defining the word as an EARTHWORK is evidence about the semantic range that the English word 'fort' obscures.

claim: No translator in the pinned corpus renders pur- as a city, with one exception in 103 passages: Griffith at RV 1.173.10 renders purpati- as 'some city's lord'.
locator: 06-BRIEFS/pur-translation-standard.md section 8. Grassmann 1876-7: Burg/Burgen 84, Feste(n) 9, never Stadt. Geldner 1951: Burg(en) 79, Feste(n) 9, Bollwerk 1, Wall 1, never Stadt. Griffith 1890: fort(s) 63, castle(s) 33, stronghold(s) 5, fortress(es) 4, city 1. Renou: forteresse(s) 34, citadelle(s) 22 over 58 passages. Elizarenkova: krepost' overwhelmingly. Counts by surface-string match, not lemmatised, so indicative rather than exact.
notes: The single 'city' falls at the one locator where a political office attached to a pur is named — purpati-, 'lord of a pur' — which is precisely where an urban reading is most consequential. Geldner has Burgherr and Grassmann Burgherrn at the same place. Not five independent witnesses: Grassmann's translation is the same judgement as the Grassmann glosses (DEP-021) and Elizarenkova worked with Geldner in view (DEP-023).

claim: Griffith renders ayasa- as 'iron' in all eight of its passages; Geldner renders it 'ehern' (of ore, brass, bronze) in all eight. The two translators are systematically describing different metals, and neither argues the point.
locator: RV 1.58.8, 2.20.8, 4.27.1, 7.3.7, 7.15.14, 7.95.1, 8.100.8, 10.101.8. Griffith 'iron' 8/8. Geldner 'ehern' 8/8. Grassmann mixes: Erz at 1.58.8, Eisen at 4.27.1, ehern at the rest, and does not render the word at 7.3.7.
notes: Recorded as an OPEN CRUX with a named consequence, not as a finding either way. The two metals have different histories in South Asia, so which is meant bears on when the passages could have been composed, and a translator's single lexical habit can therefore move a chronology. No source retrieved in this unit settles it and nothing here asserts either reading. This is what constitution section 7 means by not letting the translation decide the historical question.
